task: Write one sentence of your own using the word profuse. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know profuse should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The nosebleed was brief but profuse, ruining a shirt in the thirty seconds it lasted.
Ample stops short of profuse — ample fills the need with room to spare, while profuse comes pouring past any need at all.
Torrential goes further than profuse — profuse blooms and thanks pour generously; a torrential flow overwhelms whatever tries to hold it.

Overflowing describes the container that can no longer hold its contents — the inbox, the cup, the laundry basket spilling past its rim. Profuse describes the outpouring itself, abundant flow with no container in the picture: profuse thanks, profuse sweat, profuse blooms.

Gushing is flow rushing from a single point — a burst pipe, a cut, a fan's breathless praise — with a note of losing control. Profuse pours in quantity without needing one source or any loss of control: sweat, apologies, and blossoms can all be profuse.

The theater issued a full refund when the projector failed ten minutes into the matinee.
Profuse means plentiful, abundant.
When the mayor finally conceded the scoreboard error, his praise for the visiting team turned profuse — three superlatives a sentence, delivered until an aide gently took the microphone away.
Profuse is abundance in motion — the word wants something pouring out: profuse thanks, profuse sweat, profuse blooms.
Where 'plentiful' counts a supply, profuse describes the gushing.
Profuse loves nouns that flow: thanks, apologies, sweat, blossoms, bleeding.

For countable stockpiles say plentiful or abundant; say profuse when the quantity streams out of its source — and note the fixed medical phrase profuse bleeding, where the word is standard, not literary.
